14. Proportion of the population that has convenient access to public transport disaggregated by age group, sex, and persons with disabilities 

Adapted: SDGs 11.2.1: https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/metadata/files/Metadata-11-02-01.docx 

1. Definition and method of computations 

This indicator aims to successfully monitor the use and access of public transportation systems and move towards reducing the reliance on the private means of transportation. This includes improving the access to areas with a high proportion of transport-disadvantaged groups such as the elderly citizens, physically challenged individuals, and low-income earners - and reducing the need for mobility by decreasing the number of trips and the distances travelled. The accessibility-based urban mobility paradigm also critically needs good, high-capacity public transport systems that are well-integrated in a multi-modal arrangement with public transport access points located within comfortable walking or cycling distances from homes and jobs for all. Since most public transport users walk from their trip origins to public transport stops and from public transport stops to their trip destination, local spatial availability and accessibility to these stops is often evaluated in terms of pedestrian (walk) access, as opposed to cycle access, park and ride or transfers. Hence, this metadata proposes the access to public transport to be convenient when a stop is in walking distance of 500 m from a reference point such as a home, school, work place, or market to a low capacity public transport system (e.g. bus, Bus Rapid Transit) and 1 km to a high capacity system (e.g. rail, metro, ferry). Additional criteria for defining public transport that is convenient 

can include: a. Public transport is accessible to all special-needs customers, including those who are physically, visually, and/or hearing-impaired, as well as those with temporary disabilities, the elderly, children and other people in vulnerable situations. b. Public transport with frequent service during peak travel times c. Stops present a safe and comfortable station environment The following definitions are required to define and measure convenient access to public transport. 

Public transport is defined as a shared passenger transport service that is available to the general public and is provided for the public good. It may include cars, buses, trolleys, trams, trains, subways, and ferries that are shared by strangers without prior arrangement. It may also include informal modes of transport (para-transit) - but it is noted that these are often lacking in designated routes or stops. For a city to understand the nature of their transport system and in turn make the necessary planning and investment decisions, it is recommended that each city should do an inventory of its public transport modes and their major characteristics. For cities where a mix of formal and informal transport systems exist, it is also recommended to compute the indicator at the two levels, which is critical for decision-making processes. Recent data has shown that many cities in developing regions may lack a formal public transport system, but residents still enjoy a high level of access to public transport driven by a comprehensive paratransit network which does not necessarily have designated stops. A mapping of the transport routes where these paratransit networks can stop is thus recommended, and countries are encouraged to document each type of transport mode. 

Street Network may be defined as a system of interconnected lines that represent a system of streets or roads for a given area. A street network provides the foundation for network analysis that will help to measure the pedestrian access/ walking distance of 500 m or 1 km to a public transport stop; or the network along which random informal transport modes can be accessed. Some cities have detailed data on street network, type, street design (e.g. availability of a safe walking path) or topological structure of the network. However, if such data is not available, it is proposed to use OpenStreetMap and other sources such as GORADS, ESRI Streets, etc as a baseline and fill missing gaps through digitizing of missing lines from satellite imagery (e.g. Google Earth). The major assumption in the use of these data sources is that all streets are walkable and on the same elevation level. 49 

Service Area is defined as the area served by public transport within 500 m walking distance to a low capacity system or 1 km to a high capacity system based on the street network. 

Rationale 

Member States committed themselves to the generation and use of renewable and affordable energy and sustainable and efficient transport infrastructure and services, achieving the benefits of connectivity and reducing the financial, environmental and public health costs of inefficient mobility, congestion, air pollution, urban heat island effects and noise. They also committed themselves to giving particular attention to the energy and transport needs of all people, particularly the poor and those living in informal settlements (NUA §54). Equity and inclusivity should be at the heart of this Indicator. This objective accounts for distributional considerations and places a minimum value on everyone’s travel needs, providing all, including the vulnerable, women, young, old, and disabled with at least some basic level of access through transport services and leaving “no one behind.” The ability of all individuals to access markets, employment opportunities, and service centers such as schools and hospitals, is critical to urban economic development. To achieve the goal of “convenient access” for all, urban transport systems and services need to be upgraded - and in some cases planned from scratch - in an integrated way, that ensures the balanced access of urban residents regardless of income, mode of travel, gender, race or disability status. Urban mobility should foster and enable cities to flourish, without creating over-dependence on any particular mode of travel. The concept of convenient accessibility to jobs, services and markets also allows policymakers, citizens and businesses to discuss the state of the transport system in a comprehensible, goal-oriented way – while enhancing the understanding of recommended actions to further improve the transport system in a city. Thus, the “convenient access” SDG indicator addresses a significant gap that was never addressed by the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs): directly addressing transport as a critical enabler of economic activities and social inclusion. By focusing on access to transit, this can also be aligned with sustainability goals such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions, pollutant emissions, traffic congestion, and road fatalities and injuries - since increased use of transit aligns with these goals. Broadening the basic access concept to reaching destinations (with associated services, goods, social, education, health and other opportunities associated with these destinations) for all as the ultimate goal, the full value can be achieved; though measuring this “opportunity access” is difficult, as described above. In any case, adopting a goal of convenient access tends to align with a broad objective of making cities more compact, with shorter trips and greater focus on transit, cycling and walking through better planning and the integration of land-use planning with transport planning. 

Method of Computation – Core Indicator

The identification of service areas is typically achieved using the Network Analysis operation (in Geographic Information System - GIS) by constructing lines of proximity around each public transport stop. Countries should first identify the size of the coverage area by the network distance of 500 m or 1 km (instead of using a mere buffer of 500m - equal proximity) around the transport stop. Hence, for the core indicator, public transport is considered “convenient” for those living within a 500 m walkable distance of the nearest low capacity stop and 1 km to the nearest high capacity stop. Using network distance (the walking distance computed using the street network to reach a public transport feature) will help to realistically reflect the configuration of the street network and to recognize the presence of any barriers preventing direct access to public transport features. While the service area for each stop should be created separately, all areas should be merged to create a continuous service area for all public transport modes. # Abstract 

The Associate Member Countries (AMCs) of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) face development challenges which, individually, they lack the capacity to address. In this regard they are not dissimilar to member States. Participation in regional cooperation mechanisms, such as the Caribbean Development and Cooperation Committee (CDCC), enables AMCs to benefit from technical cooperation within the framework of regional policy agendas, putting them in a better position to overcome development challenges. However, the distinct governance arrangements of these countries and territories have limited their participation. Furthermore, different statistical practices and systems have hindered their inclusion in the publications of international organizations, including ECLAC. A fuller inclusion of AMCs in international statistical compilations and databases would greatly facilitate their integration in regional cooperation more generally. 

This study presents a statistical analysis of the situation of AMCs, based on the data that is 

available, shedding light on their distinct circumstances. It reveals that while AMCs boast higher GDP 

per capita than many Caribbean member States, their economies have had low growth and are highly dependent on trade, with some territories recording concerning levels of public debt. Socially, the AMCs face an ageing population, varied poverty levels, and have disparate social protection systems. Environmentally, they face challenges due to disasters arising from natural hazards, although there has been some progress in reducing Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions through improved energy efficiency. 

Despite the challenges in harmonizing data across these diverse territories, the study demonstrates that valuable and high-quality statistics are available, from both national and international sources. However, greater efforts are needed to integrate AMC’s data into international statistical compilations. The study highlights limitations in the availability of environmental data from official sources, making it more difficult to address environmental sustainability in these territories. Through an exclusive focus on AMCs, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of their unique circumstances and underscores the importance of their inclusion in international cooperation for sustainable development. # Introduction 

The challenges faced by small Caribbean National Statistical Offices (NSOs), and statistical systems, in meeting domestic and international demands for high quality data are widely recognised. Statistical capacity is particularly limited in the 14 associate member countries (AMCs) of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC). 1 Of these, six are British Overseas Territories (Anguilla, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands), three are constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands (Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten), thre e are overseas French Departments (French Guiana, Guadeloupe, and Martinique), and two are 

territories of the United States (Puerto Rico and United States Virgin Islands). Therefore, in addition to capacity constraints, there is a greater diversity of practice among the national statistical systems of AMCs, which is a product of the differing governance arrangements and institutional support of France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. 2

In the British Overseas Territories and the constituent countries of the Netherlands, the prime responsibility for official statistics falls on NSOs, or statistical departments, which carry out the functions of NSOs. In the territories of the United States, there are also statistical agencies, the Institute of Statistics of Puerto Rico, and the Bureau of Economic Research of the United States Virgin Islands, with the United States Government also producing important statistical outputs covering these territories, most notably the population and housing census. In the three French Departments, their statistical systems are integrated with the French national statistical system, with both the National

Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies of France (INSEE) and the French Ministry of the Interior and Overseas providing a range of statistics about the overseas departments. 

As a result of the diversity of statistical practices and political landscapes among AMCs, it can be relatively difficult to integrate these countries into research and analysis on the subregion’s sustainable development, and the monitoring of progress in implementation of international agreements. In many instances, non-availability of comparable statistical information about AMCs results in the exclusion of these countries from the publications of ECLAC and other multilateral agencies. However, this lack of visibility can also be due to oversight, a lack of familiarity with data sources for AMCs, language barriers, or insufficient engagement with the governments and statistical offices of these countries and their data. This is a barrier to more effective engagement, participation, and integration of AMCs in the regional sustainable development agenda, to the detriment of both associate members and member States alike. 

The study addresses this imbalance through the presentation of an analysis of the economic, social and environmental situation of AMCs based on a compilation of statistics focused exclusively on these countries. The study draws on official statistics collected and published by international organizations and national authorities. 

Chapter I analyses the economic situation of AMCs, their performance over the last decade, and key drivers of their economies. The chapter also analyses their dependence on trade; the strength of their labour markets; the recent reemergence of high inflation; and growing government debt levels. Chapter II analyses the social situation of AMCs. It analyses the population trends in these countries, such as their ageing populations and the impact of migration; rates of poverty and inequality; their social protection and education systems; and population health, paying particular attention to non-communicable diseases and their risk factors. Sustainable economic and social development is not possible without environmental sustainability and Chapter III analyses the environmental situation of AMCs, specifically the impact of disasters in these countries, their progress regarding the energy transition, and the issue of air quality. Finally, Chapter IV considers how AMCs can be better integrated into international statistical compilations to facilitate their participation in, and ensure that they benefit from, regional cooperation activities for advancing the regional sustainable development agenda. # I. The economic situation in associate member countries 

As Small Island Developing States (SIDS), Caribbean countries possess open economies mainly characterized by a primary reliance on tourism and trade. External shocks, ranging from financial crises, pandemics, climate change impacts and environmental disasters to downturns in global demand directly affect the sustainability of economic growth in the countries of the subregion. This vulnerability to negative external shocks naturally leads to a relatively large degree of volatility in gross domestic product 

(GDP) (figure 1). The main challenge for Caribbean SIDS is building resilience to external shocks, such as the 2008 international financial crisis, the 2017 hurricanes Irma and Maria, or the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, so that these shocks do not stifle economic growth in the long-term (Beshudi, 2020). 

Despite their status as territories, countries or constituent parts of developed countries, AMCs share economic, social, and environmental vulnerabilities similar to other SIDS. 3 With the exception of Puerto Rico which has a population of 3.26 million, AMCs have populations under 400,000 inhabitants. The small size of AMCs creates diseconomies of scale. Moreover, their economies are not diversified enough, making them dependent on tourism or, in some cases, financial services. Furthermore, weak economic growth in recent years has resulted in reduced revenues hindering the ability of governments to build resilience against external shocks. 

This chapter analyses the economic performance of AMCs by examining gross domestic product 

(GDP) , the industries driving economic growth, the trade and current account balance, labour market indicators, inflation rates, and the public debt levels of these countries. 

## A. Economic performance and drivers of growth 

According to the data presented in the Preliminary Overview of the Economies of Latin America and the Caribbean 2023, the region is projected to see slowing economic growth through to 2024.

However, higher commodity and consumer prices for food and energy security and downside risks associated with persistent inflation and tighter monetary policy are likely to contribute to maintaining lower growth trends in the Caribbean in the short-term (Durant, 2024).

Figure 1 illustrates the volatility of annual growth across AMCs over the last decade. This makes clear the negative impact of the pandemic, which had the biggest impacts on Anguilla (-30% in 2020), Turks and Caicos Islands (-27%), Aruba (-24%) and Curaçao (-18%), all among the most heavily tourism dependent economies. Among the seven AMCs shown in table 1, three were heavily dependent on financial services 

industries (Financial intermediation): British Virgin Islands (25% of GVA), the Cayman Islands (31%), and 

Curaçao (24%). The Turks and Caicos Islands (14%) exhibits a more moderate dependency on the financial service industry. Progress in the implementation of agreements between Caribbean AMCs and countries of 

the Global North , aimed at regulating offshore banking, has resulted in some Caribbean AMCs being removed from black and grey lists of non-cooperative tax jurisdictions, which is important for the development of the financial services sector and necessary for bolstering its contribution to the economic growth of these countries. In October 2023, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), created by the G -7 group of major industrialized economies, delisted the Cayman Islands from its grey list after this AMC successfully implemented mechanisms to sanction money laundering (Cayman Islands, 2023). The British Virgin Islands has also cooperated with the FATF to improve its legal framework regarding anti-money laundering and terrorism financing regulations (British Virgin Islands, 2023a). International cooperation between AMCs and other international organizations has achieved the removal of Caribbean countries from these black and grey tax lists. For example, Aruba, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands, and the Turks and Caicos Islands were removed from the European Union’s blacklist of non-cooperative tax jurisdictions, countries deemed to have regulation frameworks conducive to money laundering. However, as of early 2024, Anguilla and the United States Virgin Islands remain on this blacklist of the European Union (Council of the European Union, 2024).

Service industries in small island countries, such as tourism and financial services, help promote resilient and sustainable economic growth. In many countries worldwide, the knowledge-intensive service sector contributes to economic growth by creating technological spillovers that increase productivity in manufacturing (Pereira, Missio, and Jayme Jr., 2023). However, the small size of the economies of AMCs, apart from Puerto Rico, limits opportunities for the scaling up of manufacturing. This situation leaves the service industry as the main engine of economic growth. This lack of diversification makes AMCs more vulnerable to negative external shocks, such as climate events and international economic downturns. 

A strategy adopted by AMCs is to further specialize in their existing service industries and develop the downstream possibilities of financial services or tourism. For example, the Government of Bermuda has developed a regulatory framework for financial technology (FinTech) as it seeks to attract investments in this area to further develop its financial services sector (Bermuda, 2024b). To improve its tourist offering, the Government is also leveraging technology to bridge gaps in public transportation through the development of a rideshare application which will benefit residents and tourists alike (Bermuda, 2024c). The Government of the British Virgin Islands is working within the framework of the Organization of Eastern Caribbean States (OECS) Common Tourism Policy to develop sustainable and climate-resilient tourism and opportunities in the blue economy (British Virgin Islands, 2024). 

The energy transition also provides opportunities for specialization and resilience-building in the service sector. Encouraging private entrepreneurs in the Caribbean to switch to electric vehicles, recharged from renewable energy sources, reduces the vulnerability of the private sector to international shocks to the price of crude oil (Loayza, 2023). Martinique is investing in a new fibre optic telecommunications network, which will gradually replace the old copper network between 2023 and 2030. It will provide faster, more reliable internet connectivity that is more resilient to the elements and consumes four times less electricity than digital subscriber line (DSL) (Martinique, 2023). This is an example of how governments of the subregion can foster the resilience of service industries by providing the necessary infrastructure for private businesses to operate, especially digital and sustainable transport infrastructures that assure and facilitate international connectivity (Leon, 2022). 

## B. Trade and the balance of payments 

Trade plays an important role in the economic development of small island economies. Their small size makes them reliant on importing goods for domestic consumption and high transport costs inflate the price of these consumer goods (UNCTAD, 2016). For sustainable growth, exports are crucial so that businesses can expand, take advantage of economies of scale, and improve productivity, while providing the economy with a source of foreign exchange. A high level of imports relative to exports causes a strain on the current account balance, which affects a country’s ability to import and service external debt, which undermines the value of their currency. Examining total trade, total trade balance, the current account balance, and the net balance of trade in merchandise and commercial services for AMCs provides insight into the contribution of trade to their economic development and the vulnerabilities associated with their trade balance. 

As depicted in table 2, data from ten AMCs show that their total trade (exports plus imports of goods and services ) as a percentage of their GDP from 2012 to 2022 has been higher than the LAC 

average for all these countries. AMCs also showed higher trade intensity than Caribbean member 

States, with total trade as a share of GDP being higher than the average for Caribbean member States for all AMCs apart from Bermuda. Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten and United States Virgin Islands had particularly high trade intensity figures. The main economic threat of trade deficits for countries is that they are the main contributor to current account deficits. Such persistent and substantial deficits can lead to a balance of payments crisis. As depicted in table 4, Caribbean member States had on average low current account deficits (as a proportion 

of GDP) for most of the years between 2012 to 2022, except for 2013 and 2022 when they showed current account surpluses. Unsurprisingly, the year with the highest current account deficit for these countries was 

in 2020 (8.4% of GDP) because of the COVID -19 pandemic. As for the eight AMCs, for which data was available, two groups emerge: AMCs that exhibited current account surpluses or current accounts that were close to being balanced from 2012, and countries with persistent and substantial current account deficits. Aruba, Bermuda, Sint Maarten, and Turks and Caicos Islands belong to the first group. The current account balances for Bermuda and Turks and Caicos Islands were consistently positive over this period. Aruba showed an average current account balance of -0.4% of GDP and Sint Maarten had an average balance close to zero from 2012 to 2019, before recording deficits in excess of 20% in 2021 and 2022 due to the pandemic. In contrast, the second group of countries, Anguilla, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, and Montserrat ran persistent current account deficits in double digits during the period 2012 to 2022 (although Montserrat had current account surpluses in 2019 and 2020).

It is important to note that the implication of a balance of payments crisis can differ significantly for AMCs due to their varying currency arrangements. For instance, in countries with their own currency, such a crisis often leads to fast devaluation and a currency crisis. However, in AMCs sharing common currencies or where the currency is issued by their administrative power, the implications are different. For example, Curaçao and Sint Maarten use the Netherlands Antillean guilder, while Anguilla and Montserrat use the Eastern Caribbean dollar (ECD). Other AMCs use the Euro or US dollar. These AMCs have to operate within the constraints imposed by their use of these currencies, but they are more insulated from currency devaluation. 

The current account surpluses in Aruba and Turks and Caicos, from 2012 to 2022, were driven by persistent trade surpluses (tables 3 and 4). Sint Maarten ran a current account surplus from 2012 to 2018 and a current account deficit from 2019 to 2022, driven by a period of trade surpluses (an average surplus of 2.7% from 2012 to 2017) followed by a period of deficits (an average trade deficit of 8.7% from 2018 to 2022). However, Anguilla, Curaçao, and Montserrat ran consistently high current account deficits due to high trade deficits (at least 20% on average) from 2012 to 2022. substantial current account deficits creates vulnerabilities to the sustainable economic development of these countries such as an increased reliance on foreign capital and, depending on the currency that they use, a heightened risk of devaluation. 

However, Bermuda and the Cayman Islands are distinct as their current account balances do not correspond with the trade balances in these countries. Bermuda ran persistent trade deficits and current account surpluses, both in double digits, and Cayman Islands ran persistent trade surpluses and current account deficits (tables 3 and 4). Other financial inflows and outflows beyond trade drive the current account balances in these countries. Bermuda was a substantial recipient of remittances, which were propor tional to about 20% of its GDP from 2010 to 2020 (Leon and Abdulkadri, 2024), creating a current 

account surplus. On the other hand, in the Cayman Islands, the average annual remittances outflow 

from 2016 to 2021 was of about 8.2% of GDP (World bank, 2024) , which created a current account deficit in the country. 

Most AMCs are net merchandise or goods importers. The net trade deficit in goods as a 

percentage of GDP is in double digits for all the countries shown in table 5. The average net trade deficit in merchandize for these AMCs was 39% of GDP over the period 2012 to 2022, which was significantly 

higher than for Caribbean member States. For instance, exports in merchandise as a proportion of GDP 

was less than 5% in Anguilla, Bermuda, Cayman Islands, and Turks and Caicos Islands. However, some AMCs have more substantial merchandize exports, even if they were net importers. Merchandise 

exports in Curaçao, Montserrat, and Sint Maarten were over 10% of GDP over this period. In Curaçao, exports in goods averaged 18% of GDP from 2012 to 2022 (table A 1.6).

## C. The labour market 

The sustainability of economic growth is directly tied to the labour market and, specifically, the productivity and utilization of the labour force. For the LAC region, the unemployment rate in 2022 (7%) was one percentage point lower than the pre-pandemic rate in 2019 (8%). The labour market participation rate of 62.4% in 2022 represented a recovery almost to the pre-pandemic level (63.4% in 2019). However, the pace of this recovery seems to have stalled at levels that are far from the desired outcome, with wide gender gaps and informality continuing to characterize the region’s labour markets (ECLAC-ILO, 2023). 

Among AMCs, where economies are primarily service-based, economic growth is intrinsically linked with increased labour market participation of women in relation to men (Lechman and Kaur, 2015). Labour market participation rates for men are generally much higher than for women due to social norms that recognize men as the family’s breadwinner and women as the default provider of unpaid care work at home 

(Stuart, Gény, and Abdulkadri, 2017). 

In all AMCs, men have a higher labour market participation rate than women 15 years of age and older (figure 4). However, in half of the AMCs examined (Anguilla, Aruba, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands), the gender gap in labour participation rates is 10% or lower. The gender gap in labour participation rates, to the detriment of women, are 17% in Caribbean member States and 24% for 

the LAC region. In the British Virgin Islands, French Guiana, and Sint Maarten, the gender ga p in labour participation is 12%, still lower than the average gender gap of Caribbean member States. Only Puerto Rico (20%) and the United States Virgin Islands (21%) have a higher gender gap in labour market participation rates than in Caribbean member States. 

Puerto Rico and the United States Virgin Islands exhibited labour market participation rates of 32% and 45%, respectively, for women and labour market participation rates of 52% and 66%, respectively, for men. These participation rates are lower than the averages for women and men in Caribbean member states 

(53% and 69%, respectively), which points to weak labour markets for both genders. French Guiana displayed 

a relatively narrow gender gap in labour market participation (just over 11%), but their total labour market participation rate of 54%, below the total Caribbean member States average of about 61%, also indicates a weak labour market. 8

The economic literature assumes that service industry jobs lower labour market participation gaps between men and women in comparison to jobs in the manufacturing industries, which have historically been disproportionally occupied by men due to social norms (Lechman and Kaur, 2015). Employment in hotels and restaurants and financial intermediation in Anguilla, Aruba, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands likely contributes to the lower gender gaps in labour market participation (less than 10%) in these AMCs (figure 4). 

There are significant variations in the level of unemployment between AMCs, but the lack of regular annual data makes it difficult to assess whether there has been any overall reduction in the level of unemployment. Caribbean member States saw a decline in the unemployment rate to 6%, from about 13% in 2001 (World Bank, 2024). Some AMCs, including Bermuda, Cayman Islands and the United States Virgin Islands saw falling unemployment in the 2010s and then a pandemic-related spike in unemployment (table 8). T he British Caribbean AMCs had the largest improvements. As the GDP of 

AMCs primarily depends on the service sector, and especially the tourism industry, the 2008 global financial crisis produced a period of cyclical unemployment. The international oil price bust in late 2014 resulted in reduced fuel prices, which incentivized increased demand in the tourism industry and lower international freight shipping charges, which improved Caribbean AMCs’ terms of trade and employment rates (Hesami and others, 2020). 

However, Curaçao and the French AMCs showed a different trend in annual unemployment rates compared to the other AMCs, with higher levels of unemployment: 13% in Curaçao in 2022, 

and 18% in Guadeloupe, 13% in French Guiana, and 11% in Martinique, all in 2023. In the French 

AMCs, this represented an improvement with unemployment having fallen from around 20% or even higher in 2014. The high unemployment rates in these AMCs persisted, even as unemployment rates elsewhere fell, indicating persistent structural unemployment. Unusually low sex ratios 9 in 

Guadeloupe (83%) and Martinique (85%) may help explain the structural unemployment of these 

two countries (see table 10), as women consistently have more difficulties in joining the labour market due to social norms and the obstacles they pose to women’s entry to the labour force (Leon, Floyd, and Abdulkadri, 2023). 

Although unemployment is relatively high in the French AMCs, wages are relatively high. Average net hourly wages 10  in 2022 were approximately 15 euros in Guadeloupe, French Guiana, and Martinique 

(compared to 16.4 for France as a whole). 11  The gender gap in salaries is also lower in Guadeloupe, 

French Guiana, and Martinique (women earn 1.1%, 2.9%, and 9% less than men in these AMCs, 

respectively) compared to the national French gender pay gap of 18.1% (IEDOM, 2023c). Furthermore, the net minimum wage in Euros (after deduction of statutory social insurance payments) of the three French Caribbean AMCs was 9.23 Euros as of 2024 (Republique Française, 2024), close to two thirds of the average net hourly wages in these three overseas departments. 

Several British and Dutch AMCs have enacted minimum wage legislations in the last decade. 

The hourly minimum wage in Anguilla, British Virgin Islands, and Cayman Islands is US$ 6.00. However, a minimum wage earner working 40 hours a week earns US$ 960.00 gross per month in Anguilla, 

British Virgin Islands, and Cayman Islands, much lower than a minimum wage earner in any of the French AMCs. In the Cayman Islands, where the minimum wage is 28% of the average hourly wage, the 

Government recently created a g overnmental committee to review the minimum wage that has remained static since 2016 (Anguilla, 2023; British Virgin Islands, 2023b; Cayman Islands, 2024).

## D. Consumer price inflation 

SDG 8 calls on countries to prevent periods of runaway inflation that threaten sustainable economic growth. Prior to the post-pandemic outbreak of inflation, the Caribbean subregion had experienced a decade of low inflation, with annual increases in the consumer price index averaging little more than 1% per year. This was a consequence of low inflation in the price of imported goods and relatively weak economic growth in the subregion. 12  The trends in inflation in AMCs over this period were broadly similar to those in member States (see table 9). 

In 2021, and particularly in 2022, inflation rates increased among all AMCs, as they did for Caribbean member States. The highest inflation rates were seen in Cayman Islands (9.5%), Curaçao (7%) and United States Virgin Islands (10%), while more moderate rates were seen in Bermuda (4%), Montserrat (3%) and Sint Maarten (4%), all in 2022. The average inflation rate in 2022 across AMCs was very similar to that in Caribbean member States (6%). The reasons for these inflationary pressures were increased international oil prices due to the war in Ukraine and international supply chain constraints caused by lockdown-induced production downturns, particularly in Asia, during the pandemic (Pantin, 2022).

AMC governments, for example in Aruba, Guadeloupe, and Martinique , have implemented inflation-reducing measures, such as strengthening price controls, although on limited items such as certain food staples, medicines, and education costs (Aruba, 2024c; IEDOM, 2023a; IEDOM, 2023c). is likely that the normalization of GDP growth rates in the years following the post -pandemic economic recovery, particularly for tourism-dependent Caribbean countries, will see inflationary pressures moderate from the highs recorded in 2022 (Rosenblatt and others, 2023), although it is uncertain if the ultra-low inflation environment of 2012 to 2020 will return.

## E. Public debt 

The Caribbean is one of the most indebted subregions globally. Caribbean member States had an average debt-to-GDP ratio of 90% in 2021 (figure 5). This is higher than the 64% threshold identified for emerging economies in a World Bank study, above which such high debt-to-GDP ratios begin to jeopardize the sustainability of an emerging country’s economic development (Caner, Grennes, and Koehler -Geib , 2011). The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated global recession in 2020 would have contributed to these heightened debt levels, affecting many emerging market and developing economies (Kose, Nagle, Ohnsorge and Sugawana, 2021). For 11 AMCs of the subregion, the average debt-to-GDP 

ratio was below the recommended threshold at approximately 38%. This average shows that the economies of these AMCs are more financially stable than those of Caribbean member States.

Furthermore, Puerto Rico, as an AMC, has made significant strides in reducing its debt-to-GDP ratio and 

thus improving the economic sustainability of its public finances. A federally legislated debt restructuring agreement termed the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA Act) between Puerto Rico and the United States in 2022 reduced Puerto Rico’s debt-to-GDP ratio from approximately 56% in 2022 to 25% in 2023 (GAO, 2023). The British Virgin Islands has recently started an 

assessment of its government debt, with the support of The Commonwealth, to evaluate ways of improving debt management operations, which can help reduce overall debt levels (The Commonwealth, 2023). However, the debt-to-GDP ratio of this country is less than 20%, which is almost half the debt ratio average of AMCs (figure 5). Nevertheless, such endeavours by AMC governments help keep debt levels manageable.

# II. The social situation in associate member countries 

Caribbean countries are often described as small and open, and this is especially true of AMCs. They tend to be smaller than member States both in terms of land area and population. In addition, their non-independent status tends to reinforce the integration of their economics and societies with those of their respective administering Power or the State of which they are part. At the same time, they are an integral part of the subregion with an essential role to play in its sustainable development. The flows of intra-Caribbean migrants to and from AMCs is one example of this. This chapter addresses the social pillar of development. It starts with an analysis of key population dynamics impacting AMCs and then assesses progress in the fields of poverty reduction, social protection, education and health. 

## A. Population dynamics 

The fourteen AMCs have a total population of around 5 million persons compared to the 7.5 million living in the thirteen member States (table 10). Seven of the 14 AMCs have populations of under 100,000 inhabitants, although the three French AMCs all have populations between approximately 300 to 400 thousand, while Puerto Rico’s population (3.26 million) is larger than that of Jamaica (United Nations, 2022). The AMCs also tend to be more densely populated with 51.9 persons per square kilometre compared to 18.7 among the Caribbean member States. In all cases, the continental countries have much lower population densities than the islands. 

French Guiana has a population density of 3.6 persons per square kilometre and, like Guyana and Suriname , is among the most sparsely populated countries in the world. Excluding all continental countries, population density among the associate members is 336 persons per square kilometre compared to 231 among Caribbean member States. The AMCs with the highest population density are Sint Maarten (1,295 per square km) and Bermuda (1,189 per square km), which are also among the most densely populated countries in the world. 

There are a number of AMCs with sex ratios substantially different from 100. Aruba (89.1), Guadeloupe 

(82.7), Martinique (85.4), Puerto Rico (89.5) and United States Virgin Islands (87.8) all have sex ratios below 90, signifying that there are fewer than 90 men for every 100 females. The relatively large stocks of female migrants living in these countries, compared to male migrants, has contributed to this imbalance. Montserrat (111.8) and Sint Maarten (115.2) have excesses of males, in the case of Montserrat due to the emigration of females. Demographic ageing is generally more advanced in AMCs than in Caribbean member States and the region more generally. This means that populations in AMCs are characterised by greater longevity, lower fertility rates, lower population growth, and a relatively older population structure. The fertility rate among Caribbean AMCs is 1.56 compared to 1.67 among member States (and a replacement rate of approximately 2.1). Six AMCs have fertility rates below 1.5: Anguilla (1.27), Aruba (1.18), Bermuda (1.36), British Virgin Islands (1.01), Cayman Islands (1.22) and Puerto Rico (1.29). In contrast, the three French AMCs have higher fertility rates: French Gu iana (3.51), Guadeloupe (2.05) and Martinique (1.92). 

With fertility rates having fallen to these levels, population growth rates have also been on the decline. The population growth rate among AMCs in 2021 was -0.15% compared to a population growth rate of 0.36% among Caribbean member States. In 2021, five AMCs had negative population growth: 

Guadeloupe , Martinique, Montserrat, Puerto Rico and United States Virgin Islands. The highest population growth rates were in French Guiana (2.2%) and Turks and Caicos Islands (1.8%). It should be noted that for small countries in particular, migration also has a significant impact on population growth. For example, i n the case of Guadeloupe and Martinique, although their fertility rates are relatively close to replacement level, outward migration results in a falling population (see below). 

Increased longevity and declining fertility lead to an older population age structure. This is evident in the higher median age of the populations of AMCs (42 years) which is over ten years higher than that of m ember States (31). The only AMC with a young population is French Guiana. Its median 

age is 24 which is 12 years younger than the AMC with the second lowest median age, Curaçao (36). 

As populations age, older persons form an increasing share of the total population. This has implications for public finances as the need for expenditure on pensions and healthcare increases in ECLAC - Studies and Perspectives series-The Caribbean No. 129 Development profile of ECLAC associate members… 31 

relation to the tax revenues which are raised primarily from the working-age population. In this context, preventing the labour force participation rate from falling too far becomes an important policy consideration. An ageing population also strains the care economy, which disproportionally affects women, as they are more likely to exit the labour market to care for older persons (Leon, Floyd, and Abdulkadri, 2023). 

The old-age dependency ratio (the ratio of the population aged 65 and over to the population aged between 20 and 64 years old) measures this increase in the size of the old-age population relative to the population of working age. The dependency ratio for AMCs increased from 18 to 35 from 2000 to 2021, while in Caribbean member States it increased from 11 to 14 over the same period (figure 6). The AMCs which have the highest old-age dependency ratios (and which have seen the biggest increases over the period 2000 to 2021) are Bermuda, Guadeloupe , Martinique, Puerto Rico and United States Virgin Islands.

## C. Social protection systems 

The social protection systems of the British, French, Dutch and United States AMCs are more heterogeneous than those of Caribbean member States, which in large part reflects the AMC’s connections outside the region. With the exception of the Cayman Islands, the British AMCs have social protection systems similar to those found in Caribbean member States. The British AMCs have contributory social security systems which generally provide old age, survivors, disability, sickness and maternity benefits, among others. These systems did not tend to provide unemployment insurance, but the COVID-19 pandemic prompted some of these AMCs to introduce a temporary unemployment benefit, and Anguilla and Turks and Caicos Islands have now introduced an unemployment benefit permanently. As in member States, the non-contributory systems in these countries are much weaker. The system in the Cayman Islands is rather different with employee pensions regulated by the 

Government but funded and managed privately. 

The French AMCs have their own contributary social security systems which provide retirement pensions and health insurance but share common French systems for unemployment benefits and non-contributory benefits. These include the Active Solidarity Income (RSA) which guarantees a minimum income to those out of work or who have a low monthly income from work 16  (IEDOM, 2023a). Among the population aged 15 to 64, Guadeloupe has the highest rate of RSA beneficiaries ( 18.8%), followed by Martinique (16.2%) and French Guiana ( 12.6%) (compared to 5.5% in Hauts-de-France, the highest rate among the regions of mainland France). 

There are also commonalities between the social security systems of the Dutch AMCs, which offer similar benefits including a general old age pension (AOV), widow's and orphan’s insurance (AWW), accident insurance (OV) and illness insurance (ZV). There is a system of unemployment insurance in Aruba, and it was recently announced that a scheme will be introduced in Curaçao (Curaçao Chronicle, 2024), but there is currently no unemployment insurance in Sint Maarten. The social security agencies in Curaçao and Sint Maarten also provide basic health insurance (BVZ) while Aruba has a separate, and more comprehensive, general health insurance system (AZV) which covers every Aruban citizen. A feature of the Dutch Caribbean social security systems is the relatively higher contribution rates, compared with the English-speaking Caribbean, particularly the rates paid by employers. 

Puerto Rico and the United States Virgin Islands are covered under the US social security system which provides Old-Age (retirement), Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) benefits. In 2020, 84% of males and 81% of females aged 65 and over in Puerto Rico had a social security old age pension

## D. Education systems 

There is strong consensus among Caribbean education sector stakeholders regarding the need to improve the quality and relevance of education services and to raise educational standards in pre-school, technical, vocational and tertiary education. This requires particular attention to disparities associated with gender, disability, ethnicity and class which are present in Caribbean education systems. 

Internationally comparable statistics on education are compiled by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) to monitor progress towards the achievement of SDG 4 

(inclusive and equitable quality education). Table 14 presents a selection of these indicators for the six AMCs (with definitions for each of the indicators provided in the note below the table). With respect to participation in pre-primary education (SDG indicator 4.2.2 and 4.2.4), UNESCO reported that Anguilla, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, and Turks and Caicos Islands were making fast progress and only in Montserrat was there an absence of progress (see also UNESCO, 2023). 

The total net enrolment in upper secondary education is relatively high (above the LAC average) in Anguilla (96%), Cayman Islands (83%) and Montserrat (84%) but lower (below the LAC average) in British Virgin Islands (58%), Curaçao (77%) and Turks and Caicos Islands (66%). For the 5 AMCs for which data was available, enrolment in tertiary education was below the regional average, likely reflecting the relative lack of opportunities for tertiary education in these countries. In the three AMCs with sex disaggregated data, enrolment in tertiary education was skewed towards females, conforming to the Caribbean-wide pattern. 

Public expenditure on education at all levels is key for countries to achieve SDG 4 on ensuring 

quality and equitable education for all. The international benchmarks for expenditure on education are at 

least 4 to 6% of GDP (and/or 15 to 20% of public expen diture), as agreed in the Paris Declaration in 2021 (UNESCO, 2021). Data from eight AMCs, presented in figure 8, shows a mixed situation regarding this social development indicator during the 2010s. In Aruba, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Puerto Rico, government expenditure on education exceeds the 4% threshold, in the latter three exceeding the 6% threshold. In Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, and the Turks and Caicos Islands, on the other hand, expenditure falls below this level, in the case of the British Virgin Islands and the Cayman Islands, falling below 3%. 

In several AMCs, there were declines in government expenditure on education as a share of GDP, over 

this period, which should be particularly concerning for the AMCs falling below the 4% threshold. However, it should also be noted that child dependency ratios are declining in all these AMCs and therefore, over time, 

there are fewer children to educate. In those AMCs where expenditure as a percentage of GDP has fallen, this 

is mostly due to falling school rolls, rather than a reduction in the allocation of resources per pupil. This demographic factor should also be borne in mind when comparing the expenditure of AMCs to the regional average. While Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, and the Turks and Caicos Islands all 

fall below the regional average for expenditure on education as a share of GDP, these AMCs also have much 

lower child dependency ratios than the region as a whole. Adjusting expenditure on education for this demographic factor would lift these four AMCs above the regional average (but they would still remain below Aruba, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Puerto Rico). # Abstract 

The Associate Member Countries (AMCs) of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) face development challenges which, individually, they lack the capacity to address. In this regard they are not dissimilar to member States. Participation in regional cooperation mechanisms, such as the Caribbean Development and Cooperation Committee (CDCC), enables AMCs to benefit from technical cooperation within the framework of regional policy agendas, putting them in a better position to overcome development challenges. However, the distinct governance arrangements of these countries and territories have limited their participation. Furthermore, different statistical practices and systems have hindered their inclusion in the publications of international organizations, including ECLAC. A fuller inclusion of AMCs in international statistical compilations and databases would greatly facilitate their integration in regional cooperation more generally. 

This study presents a statistical analysis of the situation of AMCs, based on the data that is 

available, shedding light on their distinct circumstances. It reveals that while AMCs boast higher GDP 

per capita than many Caribbean member States, their economies have had low growth and are highly dependent on trade, with some territories recording concerning levels of public debt. Socially, the AMCs face an ageing population, varied poverty levels, and have disparate social protection systems. Environmentally, they face challenges due to disasters arising from natural hazards, although there has been some progress in reducing Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions through improved energy efficiency. 

Despite the challenges in harmonizing data across these diverse territories, the study demonstrates that valuable and high-quality statistics are available, from both national and international sources. However, greater efforts are needed to integrate AMC’s data into international statistical compilations. The study highlights limitations in the availability of environmental data from official sources, making it more difficult to address environmental sustainability in these territories. Through an exclusive focus on AMCs, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of their unique circumstances and underscores the importance of their inclusion in international cooperation for sustainable development. # Introduction 

The challenges faced by small Caribbean National Statistical Offices (NSOs), and statistical systems, in meeting domestic and international demands for high quality data are widely recognised. Statistical capacity is particularly limited in the 14 associate member countries (AMCs) of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC). 1 Of these, six are British Overseas Territories (Anguilla, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands), three are constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands (Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten), thre e are overseas French Departments (French Guiana, Guadeloupe, and Martinique), and two are 

territories of the United States (Puerto Rico and United States Virgin Islands). Therefore, in addition to capacity constraints, there is a greater diversity of practice among the national statistical systems of AMCs, which is a product of the differing governance arrangements and institutional support of France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. 2

In the British Overseas Territories and the constituent countries of the Netherlands, the prime responsibility for official statistics falls on NSOs, or statistical departments, which carry out the functions of NSOs. In the territories of the United States, there are also statistical agencies, the Institute of Statistics of Puerto Rico, and the Bureau of Economic Research of the United States Virgin Islands, with the United States Government also producing important statistical outputs covering these territories, most notably the population and housing census. In the three French Departments, their statistical systems are integrated with the French national statistical system, with both the National

Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies of France (INSEE) and the French Ministry of the Interior and Overseas providing a range of statistics about the overseas departments. 

As a result of the diversity of statistical practices and political landscapes among AMCs, it can be relatively difficult to integrate these countries into research and analysis on the subregion’s sustainable development, and the monitoring of progress in implementation of international agreements. In many instances, non-availability of comparable statistical information about AMCs results in the exclusion of these countries from the publications of ECLAC and other multilateral agencies. However, this lack of visibility can also be due to oversight, a lack of familiarity with data sources for AMCs, language barriers, or insufficient engagement with the governments and statistical offices of these countries and their data. This is a barrier to more effective engagement, participation, and integration of AMCs in the regional sustainable development agenda, to the detriment of both associate members and member States alike. 

The study addresses this imbalance through the presentation of an analysis of the economic, social and environmental situation of AMCs based on a compilation of statistics focused exclusively on these countries. The study draws on official statistics collected and published by international organizations and national authorities. 

Chapter I analyses the economic situation of AMCs, their performance over the last decade, and key drivers of their economies. The chapter also analyses their dependence on trade; the strength of their labour markets; the recent reemergence of high inflation; and growing government debt levels. Chapter II analyses the social situation of AMCs. It analyses the population trends in these countries, such as their ageing populations and the impact of migration; rates of poverty and inequality; their social protection and education systems; and population health, paying particular attention to non-communicable diseases and their risk factors. Sustainable economic and social development is not possible without environmental sustainability and Chapter III analyses the environmental situation of AMCs, specifically the impact of disasters in these countries, their progress regarding the energy transition, and the issue of air quality. Finally, Chapter IV considers how AMCs can be better integrated into international statistical compilations to facilitate their participation in, and ensure that they benefit from, regional cooperation activities for advancing the regional sustainable development agenda. # I. The economic situation in associate member countries 

As Small Island Developing States (SIDS), Caribbean countries possess open economies mainly characterized by a primary reliance on tourism and trade. External shocks, ranging from financial crises, pandemics, climate change impacts and environmental disasters to downturns in global demand directly affect the sustainability of economic growth in the countries of the subregion. This vulnerability to negative external shocks naturally leads to a relatively large degree of volatility in gross domestic product 

(GDP) (figure 1). The main challenge for Caribbean SIDS is building resilience to external shocks, such as the 2008 international financial crisis, the 2017 hurricanes Irma and Maria, or the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, so that these shocks do not stifle economic growth in the long-term (Beshudi, 2020). 

Despite their status as territories, countries or constituent parts of developed countries, AMCs share economic, social, and environmental vulnerabilities similar to other SIDS. 3 With the exception of Puerto Rico which has a population of 3.26 million, AMCs have populations under 400,000 inhabitants. The small size of AMCs creates diseconomies of scale. Moreover, their economies are not diversified enough, making them dependent on tourism or, in some cases, financial services. Furthermore, weak economic growth in recent years has resulted in reduced revenues hindering the ability of governments to build resilience against external shocks. 

This chapter analyses the economic performance of AMCs by examining gross domestic product 

(GDP) , the industries driving economic growth, the trade and current account balance, labour market indicators, inflation rates, and the public debt levels of these countries. 

## A. Economic performance and drivers of growth 

According to the data presented in the Preliminary Overview of the Economies of Latin America and the Caribbean 2023, the region is projected to see slowing economic growth through to 2024.

This represents a normalization following the high growth rates registered in 2021 as economies rebounded from the COVID-19-related lockdowns of 2020 (ECLAC, 2023a). In the Caribbean, a recovery of the tourism sector drove this return to growth and the debt-to-GDP ratio improved, after spiking in 2020, (Durant, 2024). In the Caribbean, 4 (excluding Guyana) , GDP growth is projected to be 3.4% for 2023 compared to 6.4% in 2022. This represents a better economic situation than the corresponding figures of 2.2% for the Latin America and Caribbean (LAC) region in 2023, down from 4.0% in 2022 (ECLAC, 2023a). However, higher commodity and consumer prices for food and energy security and downside risks associated with persistent inflation and tighter monetary policy are likely to contribute to maintaining lower growth trends in the Caribbean in the short-term (Durant, 2024).

Hotel and restaurants contributed substantial proportions of GVA in Anguilla (21%), Aruba (19%), 

and the Turks and Caicos Islands (26%), reflecting the importance of tourism to these countries. This 

industry provided about 8% of GVA in the British Virgin Islands and Curaçao, a nd just 3% in the Cayman Islands and Montserrat. The SDG framework recognizes the importance of tourism in 

promoting sustainable economic growth, as enshrined in SDG target 8.9 calling on countries to devise 

and implement policies to p romote sustainable tourism. Indicator 8.9.1 of this SDG target is the proportion that tourism directly contributes to the GDP of a country. The World Travel and Tourism 

Council (WTTC) publish estimates of the total economic contribution of tourism which, in addition to 

Hotels and restaurants , includes all other goods and services purchased by tourists. The latest available data for 2019 suggest that the direct economic contribution of tourism to the economies of AMCs (15.5 US$ billions) was almost as large as for Caribbean member States (18.4 US$ billions) (WTTC, 2022). According to WTTC, six AMCs have a high dependence on travel and tourism: Anguilla (49% of GDP), 

Aruba (68%), British Virgin Islands (44%), Cayman Islands (21%), Curaçao (26%), and the United States Virgin Islands (29%). Other AMCs depend less on travel and tourism: Bermuda (16%),

Service industries in small island countries, such as tourism and financial services, help promote resilient and sustainable economic growth. In many countries worldwide, the knowledge-intensive service sector contributes to economic growth by creating technological spillovers that increase productivity in manufacturing (Pereira, Missio, and Jayme Jr., 2023). However, the small size of the economies of AMCs, apart from Puerto Rico, limits opportunities for the scaling up of manufacturing. This situation leaves the service industry as the main engine of economic growth. This lack of diversification makes AMCs more vulnerable to negative external shocks, such as climate events and international economic downturns. 

A strategy adopted by AMCs is to further specialize in their existing service industries and develop the downstream possibilities of financial services or tourism. For example, the Government of Bermuda has developed a regulatory framework for financial technology (FinTech) as it seeks to attract investments in this area to further develop its financial services sector (Bermuda, 2024b). To improve its tourist offering, the Government is also leveraging technology to bridge gaps in public transportation through the development of a rideshare application which will benefit residents and tourists alike (Bermuda, 2024c). The Government of the British Virgin Islands is working within the framework of the Organization of Eastern Caribbean States (OECS) Common Tourism Policy to develop sustainable and climate-resilient tourism and opportunities in the blue economy (British Virgin Islands, 2024). 

The energy transition also provides opportunities for specialization and resilience-building in the service sector. Encouraging private entrepreneurs in the Caribbean to switch to electric vehicles, recharged from renewable energy sources, reduces the vulnerability of the private sector to international shocks to the price of crude oil (Loayza, 2023). Martinique is investing in a new fibre optic telecommunications network, which will gradually replace the old copper network between 2023 and 2030. It will provide faster, more reliable internet connectivity that is more resilient to the elements and consumes four times less electricity than digital subscriber line (DSL) (Martinique, 2023). This is an example of how governments of the subregion can foster the resilience of service industries by providing the necessary infrastructure for private businesses to operate, especially digital and sustainable transport infrastructures that assure and facilitate international connectivity (Leon, 2022). 

## B. Trade and the balance of payments 

Trade plays an important role in the economic development of small island economies. Their small size makes them reliant on importing goods for domestic consumption and high transport costs inflate the price of these consumer goods (UNCTAD, 2016). For sustainable growth, exports are crucial so that businesses can expand, take advantage of economies of scale, and improve productivity, while providing the economy with a source of foreign exchange. A high level of imports relative to exports causes a strain on the current account balance, which affects a country’s ability to import and service external debt, which undermines the value of their currency. Examining total trade, total trade balance, the current account balance, and the net balance of trade in merchandise and commercial services for AMCs provides insight into the contribution of trade to their economic development and the vulnerabilities associated with their trade balance. 

As depicted in table 2, data from ten AMCs show that their total trade (exports plus imports of goods and services ) as a percentage of their GDP from 2012 to 2022 has been higher than the LAC 

average for all these countries. AMCs also showed higher trade intensity than Caribbean member 

States, with total trade as a share of GDP being higher than the average for Caribbean member States for all AMCs apart from Bermuda. Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten and United States Virgin Islands had particularly high trade intensity figures. The main economic threat of trade deficits for countries is that they are the main contributor to current account deficits. Such persistent and substantial deficits can lead to a balance of payments crisis. As depicted in table 4, Caribbean member States had on average low current account deficits (as a proportion 

of GDP) for most of the years between 2012 to 2022, except for 2013 and 2022 when they showed current account surpluses. Unsurprisingly, the year with the highest current account deficit for these countries was 

in 2020 (8.4% of GDP) because of the COVID -19 pandemic. As for the eight AMCs, for which data was available, two groups emerge: AMCs that exhibited current account surpluses or current accounts that were close to being balanced from 2012, and countries with persistent and substantial current account deficits. Aruba, Bermuda, Sint Maarten, and Turks and Caicos Islands belong to the first group. The current account balances for Bermuda and Turks and Caicos Islands were consistently positive over this period. Aruba showed an average current account balance of -0.4% of GDP and Sint Maarten had an average balance close to zero from 2012 to 2019, before recording deficits in excess of 20% in 2021 and 2022 due to the pandemic. In contrast, the second group of countries, Anguilla, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, and Montserrat ran persistent current account deficits in double digits during the period 2012 to 2022 (although Montserrat had current account surpluses in 2019 and 2020).

It is important to note that the implication of a balance of payments crisis can differ significantly for AMCs due to their varying currency arrangements. For instance, in countries with their own currency, such a crisis often leads to fast devaluation and a currency crisis. However, in AMCs sharing common currencies or where the currency is issued by their administrative power, the implications are different. For example, Curaçao and Sint Maarten use the Netherlands Antillean guilder, while Anguilla and Montserrat use the Eastern Caribbean dollar (ECD). Other AMCs use the Euro or US dollar. These AMCs have to operate within the constraints imposed by their use of these currencies, but they are more insulated from currency devaluation. 

The current account surpluses in Aruba and Turks and Caicos, from 2012 to 2022, were driven by persistent trade surpluses (tables 3 and 4). Sint Maarten ran a current account surplus from 2012 to 2018 and a current account deficit from 2019 to 2022, driven by a period of trade surpluses (an average surplus of 2.7% from 2012 to 2017) followed by a period of deficits (an average trade deficit of 8.7% from 2018 to 2022). However, Anguilla, Curaçao, and Montserrat ran consistently high current account deficits due to high trade deficits (at least 20% on average) from 2012 to 2022. Bermuda ran persistent trade deficits and current account surpluses, both in double digits, and Cayman Islands ran persistent trade surpluses and current account deficits (tables 3 and 4). Other financial inflows and outflows beyond trade drive the current account balances in these countries. ## C. The labour market 

The sustainability of economic growth is directly tied to the labour market and, specifically, the productivity and utilization of the labour force. For the LAC region, the unemployment rate in 2022 (7%) was one percentage point lower than the pre-pandemic rate in 2019 (8%). The labour market participation rate of 62.4% in 2022 represented a recovery almost to the pre-pandemic level (63.4% in 2019). However, the pace of this recovery seems to have stalled at levels that are far from the desired outcome, with wide gender gaps and informality continuing to characterize the region’s labour markets (ECLAC-ILO, 2023). 

Among AMCs, where economies are primarily service-based, economic growth is intrinsically linked with increased labour market participation of women in relation to men (Lechman and Kaur, 2015). Labour market participation rates for men are generally much higher than for women due to social norms that recognize men as the family’s breadwinner and women as the default provider of unpaid care work at home 

(Stuart, Gény, and Abdulkadri, 2017). 

In all AMCs, men have a higher labour market participation rate than women 15 years of age and older (figure 4). However, in half of the AMCs examined (Anguilla, Aruba, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands), the gender gap in labour participation rates is 10% or lower. The gender gap in labour participation rates, to the detriment of women, are 17% in Caribbean member States and 24% for 

the LAC region. In the British Virgin Islands, French Guiana, and Sint Maarten, the gender ga p in labour participation is 12%, still lower than the average gender gap of Caribbean member States. Only Puerto Rico (20%) and the United States Virgin Islands (21%) have a higher gender gap in labour market participation rates than in Caribbean member States. 

Puerto Rico and the United States Virgin Islands exhibited labour market participation rates of 32% and 45%, respectively, for women and labour market participation rates of 52% and 66%, respectively, for men. These participation rates are lower than the averages for women and men in Caribbean member states 

(53% and 69%, respectively), which points to weak labour markets for both genders. French Guiana displayed 

a relatively narrow gender gap in labour market participation (just over 11%), but their total labour market participation rate of 54%, below the total Caribbean member States average of about 61%, also indicates a weak labour market. 8

The economic literature assumes that service industry jobs lower labour market participation gaps between men and women in comparison to jobs in the manufacturing industries, which have historically been disproportionally occupied by men due to social norms (Lechman and Kaur, 2015). Employment in hotels and restaurants and financial intermediation in Anguilla, Aruba, Cayman Islands, Curaçao, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands likely contributes to the lower gender gaps in labour market participation (less than 10%) in these AMCs (figure 4). 

There are significant variations in the level of unemployment between AMCs, but the lack of regular annual data makes it difficult to assess whether there has been any overall reduction in the level of unemployment. Caribbean member States saw a decline in the unemployment rate to 6%, from about 13% in 2001 (World Bank, 2024). Some AMCs, including Bermuda, Cayman Islands and the United States Virgin Islands saw falling unemployment in the 2010s and then a pandemic-related spike in unemployment (table 8). T he British Caribbean AMCs had the largest improvements. As the GDP of 

AMCs primarily depends on the service sector, and especially the tourism industry, the 2008 global financial crisis produced a period of cyclical unemployment. The international oil price bust in late 2014 resulted in reduced fuel prices, which incentivized increased demand in the tourism industry and lower international freight shipping charges, which improved Caribbean AMCs’ terms of trade and employment rates (Hesami and others, 2020). 

However, Curaçao and the French AMCs showed a different trend in annual unemployment rates compared to the other AMCs, with higher levels of unemployment: 13% in Curaçao in 2022, 

and 18% in Guadeloupe, 13% in French Guiana, and 11% in Martinique, all in 2023. In the French 

AMCs, this represented an improvement with unemployment having fallen from around 20% or even higher in 2014. The high unemployment rates in these AMCs persisted, even as unemployment rates elsewhere fell, indicating persistent structural unemployment. Unusually low sex ratios 9 in 

Guadeloupe (83%) and Martinique (85%) may help explain the structural unemployment of these 

two countries (see table 10), as women consistently have more difficulties in joining the labour market due to social norms and the obstacles they pose to women’s entry to the labour force (Leon, Floyd, and Abdulkadri, 2023). 

Although unemployment is relatively high in the French AMCs, wages are relatively high. Average net hourly wages 10  in 2022 were approximately 15 euros in Guadeloupe, French Guiana, and Martinique 

(compared to 16.4 for France as a whole). 11  The gender gap in salaries is also lower in Guadeloupe, 

French Guiana, and Martinique (women earn 1.1%, 2.9%, and 9% less than men in these AMCs, 

respectively) compared to the national French gender pay gap of 18.1% (IEDOM, 2023c). Furthermore, the net minimum wage in Euros (after deduction of statutory social insurance payments) of the three French Caribbean AMCs was 9.23 Euros as of 2024 (Republique Française, 2024), close to two thirds of the average net hourly wages in these three overseas departments. 

Several British and Dutch AMCs have enacted minimum wage legislations in the last decade. 

The hourly minimum wage in Anguilla, British Virgin Islands, and Cayman Islands is US$ 6.00. However, a minimum wage earner working 40 hours a week earns US$ 960.00 gross per month in Anguilla, 

British Virgin Islands, and Cayman Islands, much lower than a minimum wage earner in any of the French AMCs. In the Cayman Islands, where the minimum wage is 28% of the average hourly wage, the 

Government recently created a g overnmental committee to review the minimum wage that has remained static since 2016 (Anguilla, 2023; British Virgin Islands, 2023b; Cayman Islands, 2024).

## D. Consumer price inflation 

SDG 8 calls on countries to prevent periods of runaway inflation that threaten sustainable economic growth. Prior to the post-pandemic outbreak of inflation, the Caribbean subregion had experienced a decade of low inflation, with annual increases in the consumer price index averaging little more than 1% per year. This was a consequence of low inflation in the price of imported goods and relatively weak economic growth in the subregion. 12  The trends in inflation in AMCs over this period were broadly similar to those in member States (see table 9). 

In 2021, and particularly in 2022, inflation rates increased among all AMCs, as they did for Caribbean member States. The highest inflation rates were seen in Cayman Islands (9.5%), Curaçao (7%) and United States Virgin Islands (10%), while more moderate rates were seen in Bermuda (4%), Montserrat (3%) and Sint Maarten (4%), all in 2022. The average inflation rate in 2022 across AMCs was very similar to that in Caribbean member States (6%). The reasons for these inflationary pressures were increased international oil prices due to the war in Ukraine and international supply chain constraints caused by lockdown-induced production downturns, particularly in Asia, during the pandemic (Pantin, 2022).

AMC governments, for example in Aruba, Guadeloupe, and Martinique , have implemented inflation-reducing measures, such as strengthening price controls, although on limited items such as certain food staples, medicines, and education costs (Aruba, 2024c; IEDOM, 2023a; IEDOM, 2023c). It 

is likely that the normalization of GDP growth rates in the years following the post -pandemic economic recovery, particularly for tourism-dependent Caribbean countries, will see inflationary pressures moderate from the highs recorded in 2022 (Rosenblatt and others, 2023), although it is uncertain if the ultra-low inflation environment of 2012 to 2020 will return.

## E. Public debt 

The Caribbean is one of the most indebted subregions globally. Caribbean member States had an average debt-to-GDP ratio of 90% in 2021 (figure 5). This is higher than the 64% threshold identified for emerging economies in a World Bank study, above which such high debt-to-GDP ratios begin to jeopardize the sustainability of an emerging country’s economic development (Caner, Grennes, and Koehler -Geib , 2011). The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated global recession in 2020 would have contributed to these heightened debt levels, affecting many emerging market and developing economies (Kose, Nagle, Ohnsorge and Sugawana, 2021). For 11 AMCs of the subregion, the average debt-to-GDP 

ratio was below the recommended threshold at approximately 38%. This average shows that the economies of these AMCs are more financially stable than those of Caribbean member States.
